newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal PM renews threat to seek early elections.
newsitem.headline: Portugal PM renews threat to seek early elections.

text.p: Portugal's Prime Minister Antonio Guterres reaffirmed on Monday he would rather seek early elections than accept opposition plans for increased local authority funding he said meant either higher taxes or missing out on Europe's single currency.

"The government cannot accept that...opposition parties unite to force us to govern against our convictions," said Guterres, whose Socialist government is just short of an outright majority in parliament.

The Socialists say that opposition schemes, including one put forward by its principal rival, the Social Democrats, would cost some 150 billion escudos ($880 million) and could not be financed without breaking the state budget.
Reducing the budget deficit is a key condition for entry to the European Union's single currency due to be launched in 1999.
"This is something that we cannot accept...something that involves missing out on the single currency...or worse still, raising taxes drastically," Guterres said.

After first appearing to back down, Social Democrat leader Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa threw down the gauntlet to the government over the weekend, saying that his party was sticking to its proposal and challenging the government to seek a vote.

But Guterres, who took office in October 1995 for a four-year term, said he still hoped a deal could be done to avoid the calling of a general election which could itself jeopardise the country's chances of making the grade for monetary union.
"We are sensible and we hope others are, too," he said.

The government intends to present its own plans for boosting local government financing to parliament on July 9. It says that its scheme balances the increase in funding with a compensating transfer of responsibilities to ease the net cost to the state.
The issue has been thrust to the centre of political debate by the approach of local authority elections due in December.

But local financial markets have so far shrugged off the public row, with neither the stock market nor the bond market showing any reaction to the war of words because most traders expect some compromise to be found.
Although the Socialists have talked about seeking an early vote, the power to dissolve parliament rests with Portuguese President Jorge Sampaio.
